stem: A 2-year-old child presents with leukocoria and strabismus; which diagnosis should be assumed until proven otherwise?
explanation: Retinoblastoma is the diagnosis to assume until proven otherwise in a child with leukocoria, especially when strabismus is also present.

citations.source: Louisa Leone MD3 2025 - Child and Adolescent Health - Study Notes.pdf
citations.title: Louisa Leone MD3 2025 - Child and Adolescent Health - Study Notes.pdf

rationale: Retinoblastoma is the key must-not-miss cause of leukocoria in young children, and associated strabismus increases concern for intraocular pathology.

optionExplanations.A: Correct because retinoblastoma is the classic must-not-miss diagnosis for leukocoria in a young child and should be assumed until excluded.
optionExplanations.B: Incorrect because Coats’ disease can cause leukocoria but is not the diagnosis that should be presumed first in this presentation.
optionExplanations.C: Incorrect because persistent foveal vasculature is a less urgent differential and does not fit the default assumption for leukocoria.
optionExplanations.D: Incorrect because congenital cataract can cause a white reflex, but retinoblastoma must be excluded first.
optionExplanations.E: Incorrect because endophthalmitis may cause ocular inflammation, but it is not the presumptive diagnosis for leukocoria in this child.
